analysis.one_liner: Ends the tax break letting US corporations defer taxes on foreign profits; raises taxes on big oil.
analysis.headline: The bill was referred to the House Ways and Means Committee in February 2013 and never received a hearing, a vote, or any further action before the 113th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would tax the foreign profits of US corporations in the same year they are earned, instead of letting companies put off paying US tax indefinitely by keeping profits parked overseas. It would also stop large oil companies from using payments to foreign governments as tax credits, and require foreign companies that are actually run from the United States to pay US corporate tax. The bill was introduced in the House and sent to the tax-writing committee, where it sat with no action for the rest of the Congress.
analysis.who_benefits: Ordinary taxpayers, who would no longer bear a share of the cost of taxes corporations put off, and who would benefit from additional revenue that could fund public programs or reduce other taxes. Domestic-only competitors of multinationals would also face a more level playing field.

how_it_helps.text: The bill removes deferral of tax on the foreign-source income of US corporations for taxable years after December 31, 2013, meaning foreign profits would be taxed when earned rather than indefinitely postponed.

It denies the foreign tax credit to large integrated oil companies that are dual capacity taxpayers, closing a way for multibillion-dollar oil firms to reduce their US tax bill with payments to foreign governments.
It treats foreign corporations that are managed and controlled primarily in the United States as domestic corporations for US income tax purposes.

analysis.who_pays: US multinational corporations with substantial foreign profits, large integrated oil companies (over $1 billion in gross receipts and 500,000 barrels of daily production) that would lose foreign tax credit benefits, and foreign-incorporated but US-managed companies that would owe US tax. Some of these costs could be passed to consumers and shareholders, and the change could raise compliance and competitive pressures for multinationals.

drawbacks.text: Companies subject to the change warn that taxing foreign profits as they are earned can put US-headquartered multinationals at a disadvantage against foreign rivals that are not subject to US tax on their worldwide income, and that costs may be passed along to consumers through prices.

The bill changes complex rules (such as the per-country foreign tax credit limitation) that affect many legitimate cross-border businesses, and any abrupt change can create uncertainty for firms and investors until regulations are written.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill's benefit is a larger, more reliable corporate tax base and the removal of a tax preference that mainly rewards keeping profits offshore; its cost falls on multinationals and large oil companies, with some risk of higher consumer prices and competitive pressure on US firms abroad. On balance it is a revenue-raising, pro-taxpayer change, but the honest downside is that US-based multinationals would face higher compliance costs and a potential competitive disadvantage against foreign rivals not subject to US taxation.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced in February 2013 and referred to the House Ways and Means Committee, which never took it up, so it died without a hearing or vote when the 113th Congress ended in January 2015.

narrative.text: The Corporate Tax Fairness Act was introduced in the House on February 14, 2013 by Rep. Jan Schakowsky with three Democratic cosponsors.
The same day, the bill was referred to the House Committee on Ways and Means, the committee with jurisdiction over tax legislation.
No further action was taken on the bill for the remainder of the 113th Congress; it never received a hearing, a markup, or a floor vote.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: US multinational corporations and large oil companies benefited, since the tax changes the bill would have imposed on their foreign profits and foreign tax credits never took effect; taxpayers who would have gained revenue lost out.

sides.party_line_note: The bill's sponsor and all three cosponsors were Democrats, and it sat without action in committee until the Congress ended.

industries.note: The bill would eliminate deferral of US tax on their foreign-source income, meaning foreign profits would be taxed in the year earned instead of indefinitely postponed. Companies would owe tax sooner and could no longer keep profits offshore tax-free.

The bill denies the foreign tax credit to large integrated oil companies that are dual capacity taxpayers (those paying levies to foreign governments while receiving specific economic benefits from them), and limits foreign tax credit offsets. This would raise these companies' effective US tax rate on foreign operations.

The bill treats foreign corporations that are managed and controlled primarily in the United States as domestic corporations for US income tax purposes, ending a structure used to avoid US corporate tax.
Businesses competing against multinationals that defer US tax on foreign profits would face a more level tax playing field, since rivals would no longer hold an offshore tax advantage.
